The proposed answer of 18 is incorrect. The correct value is 138.

**Reduction.** Write $P(x)=\sum_j E_j (x)_j$ with $(x)_j = x(x-1)\cdots(x-j+1)$. The integer-valued condition $p^k \mid P(x)$ for all $x$ holds iff $p^{\max(0,\,k-v_p(j!))}\mid E_j$ for every $j$. The coefficient of $x^n$ in $(x)_j$ is the Stirling number $s(j,n)$, so the problem asks for integers $m_j$ with $\sum_j p^{a_j} m_j\, s(j,n)=1$, where $a_j=\max(0,\,k-v_p(j!))$. Such $m_j$ exist iff the gcd of the coefficients is 1. Checking primes $q\ne p$ is automatic (the $j=n$ term is $p^{a_n}$). For $q=p$, this requires some $j\ge n$ with $p\nmid s(j,n)$ and $v_p(j!)\ge k$. Hence
$$k(n,p)=\max\{v_p(j!) : j\ge n,\ p\nmid s(j,n)\}.$$

**Locating the maximum.** Write $j=pq+r$ with $0\le r<p$. Mod $p$, the rising factorial satisfies $x(x+1)\cdots(x+j-1)\equiv (x^p-x)^q\cdot f_r(x)$. Every term of $(x^p-x)^q$ has degree at least $q$, so a nonzero coefficient of $x^n$ forces $q\le n$. Also $v_p(j!)=q+v_p(q!)$. Taking $j=pn$ gives $s(pn,n)\equiv(-1)^n\not\equiv 0 \pmod p$, so the bound is attained:
$$k(n,p)=n+v_p(n!)\quad\text{for } n<p^2.$$

**Sanity check.** For $p=2$, $n=2$ this gives $2+1=3$, matching the known value $k(2,2)=3$ that the proposed solution itself cites. The formula $\lceil n/(p-1)\rceil$ in the proposed solution fails this check, so its derivation is unreliable.

**Computation.**
- $p=11$: $v_{11}(n!)=1$ for $n=11,\dots,15$, so $k=n+1$ gives $12+13+14+15+16=70$.
- $p=13$: $v_{13}(n!)=0$ for $n=11,12$ and $1$ for $n=13,14,15$, so $k$ gives $11+12+14+15+16=68$.

Total: $70+68=138$.
